newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Aussie dlr's rare rally wrecked by rate risk.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Aussie dlr's rare rally wrecked by rate risk.

text.p: The Australian dollar enjoyed a rare 1/2 cent rally Thursday as demand from respected Swiss and U.S. names caught the market in a classic bear squeeze.
But again the currency was handicapped by the risk of a domestic rate cut and had yet to show the sort of revival that might presage an end to its two month-old downtrend.

The market's rate anxiety shone through this morning when whispers of an imminent easing put dealers in a cold sweat. On this occasion the RBA stayed silent and speculators scurried to cover shorts, but the threat lingered and smothered the comeback before it could capture crucial resistance at US$0.7735.
Thus by 4.45 pm (0545 GMT) the local dollar had pulled back to US$0.7710/15 from a US$0.7732 high, but was still comfortably above its US$0.7673/78 close here Wednesday.

A few of the braver dealers felt the currency may have found a temporary floor here in the form of a major upward sloping trendline which stretched back to September 1993 and currently comes in around US$0.7660. This offered enough support Wednesday that the U.S. and Swiss names were encouraged to buy.
But much now depended on whether the currency could recover US$0.7735, a difficult task given that a large Asian speculator was thought to be defending an options position there.
A clear break of this barrier would point to a longer period of consolidation between here and 78 cents and raise the chance, albeit a slim one, of a recovery back above US$0.7850.
Failure would inevitably see a re-test of US$0.7660 and reinforce the risk of a retracement to 75 cents and beyond.
The story has been the reverse on most crosses where the local dollar has benefited from a world wide flow out of low yielding currencies like the yen, mark and Swiss franc.
It actually hit a 4-1/2 year high on the yen this morning at 94.70 before a senior Japanese official raised the spectre of intervention and profit-taking pulled it back to 93.70/80.
That was still a shade up on Wednesday's late 93.60/70 and brought the dollar's gains since its uptrend began in January 1996 to no less than 24 percent.
This in turn underpinned the dollar in trade weighted terms where it was up at 58.8 at midday from 58.6 late Wednesday and 54.5 this time last year.

There were signs Japan might be growing uneasy about the weakness of the yen, however. The Ministry of Finance's currency guru, Eisuke Sakakibara, said Japan would conduct intervention at an effective time when it judged that the yen's fall was really doing harm to the economy.

The comment knocked US$/yen back to 121.50/60 yen from a morning high around 122.60, but dealers doubted it would have a lasting impact as the U.S. authorities, and Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin in particular, continued to favour a firm dollar.
The local currency's biggest nightmare remained the possibility of another cut in official interest rates.

The market has been in a state of high anxiety since the RBA caught it napping with its last easing on December 11. Which was why it took fright at the rumour of a cut this morning, even though those with cooler heads thought it highly improbable the bank would cut the week before its monthly board meeting.

Analysts are split on whether the bank will decide to cut at that meeting, held on Tuesday, but a slight majority are leaning to the view it will hold off until March and see how data on wages and the real side of the economy pan out.
Today's economic figures were too mixed to offer much guidance. Skilled vacancies rose 2.1 percent in January, the first rise in 11 months, after a flat result in December.
New motor vehicle registrations for December eased 0.1 percent after a downward revised 4.7 percent gain in November, but were up 3.8 percent in annual terms.
